column3: A collective command to defend their gods directly parallels the chiefs' call to stand firm by theirs.
Its prohibition of installing another god directly counters the collective loyalty urged in the focus.
Competing intentions to lead a group into deviation illuminate the focus's claim that a new message is an intended scheme.
The immediately preceding objection rejects making many gods one and calls it astonishing.
This immediate continuation depicts the gathered factions as a defeated host.
Its steadfastness in righteous action contrasts with patience enlisted to preserve idolatry.
The repeated formula calling something astonishing offers only a verbal parallel to the focus's suspicious reaction.
Flight to God supplies the positive alternative to remaining loyal to multiple gods.
Its direct command to patience resonates, though its beautiful patience has a different object and setting.
A disbelieving elite collectively diminishes a messenger as merely human, closely matching the focus's leaders.
The surah opening frames the same passage of voiced authority and distorted reception.
Possible deceptive intent is a distant parallel to the opponents' attribution of an ulterior design.
An elite labels the threatening messenger a learned sorcerer, matching the leaders' hostile framing.
The immediate passage names prior peoples as factions, extending the focus's collective opposition.
Preparation for a military departure does not clarify idolatrous solidarity or the disputed agenda.
An arrogant elite confronts weaker believers over a messenger's authority, strongly paralleling organized resistance.
It explicitly rejects setting another god alongside God, directly opposing the focus's appeal to preserve gods.
Steadfast companionship with worshippers of God contrasts with the leaders' social discipline around idols.
The people are commanded not to abandon their named gods, a direct parallel to the focus's instruction.
The immediate predecessor records their astonishment and accusation that the warner is a lying sorcerer.
The shared command to walk has no comparable collective religious purpose.
A community's elite declares its messenger plainly astray, closely matching the focus's authoritative dismissal.
The immediate continuation makes all those peoples rejecters of messengers.
A prophet's difficulty speaking is unrelated to the leaders' mobilization or allegiance to gods.
Collective movement and hushed speech offer only a faint formal parallel to the leaders setting out.
It condemns making another god beside God, directly negating the focus's idolatrous commitment.
Opponents disparage a messenger's ordinary movement among people, paralleling hostile rhetorical resistance.
Steadfastness under threat has a collective dimension, but is directed toward God rather than idols.
The immediate successor calls the monotheistic message a fabrication, explaining the focus's alleged agenda.
The imperative to depart is used in a wholly different scene of judgment.
Mockers resent a messenger's criticism of their gods while rejecting remembrance of the Merciful.
The immediate context invokes destroyed earlier generations and their futile cry for escape.
The listed virtue of patience is too general to illuminate its politicized use in the focus.
Divine intending and bringing a thing about contrast with the opponents' vague claim that something is intended.
Creation of fire from green wood does not clarify the focus's collective religious conflict.
It exposes the helplessness of subordinate gods when the Merciful wills harm.
Its command to patient unity shows social steadfastness ordered around obedience to God, contrasting the focus's use.
The immediate successor voices their status-based objection to revelation and diagnoses their doubt.
God's effective will provides a meaningful counterpoint to the opponents' insinuation of an unnamed plan.
Moses directs an oppressed community to seek God and be steadfast, reversing the focus's elite-led idolatrous solidarity.
The immediate passage announces the single unavoidable cry awaiting the opponents.
God guides whom He wills, but this does not address the opponents' social accusation of intent.
Walking when lit and stopping in darkness faintly contrasts deliberate, leader-directed movement.
The proclamation teaches that God is one, directly countering preservation of multiple gods.
Patience and gratitude in a travel narrative are only remotely related to the focus's command to endure.
An assembly makes a collective commitment then largely withdraws, illuminating the fragility of group resolve.
The immediate context begins the catalogue of earlier rejecting powers.
Hostile plotting is a limited parallel to imputing an ulterior design to the new teaching.
Pharaoh addresses his elite, asserts exclusive divinity, and calls Moses a liar, closely matching the focus's leadership conflict.
The magicians' confession of faith in the one Lord supplies a direct reversal of attachment to many gods.
Patience as restraint before demanding access is relevant but lacks the focus's collective idolatrous aim.
A resolved divorce decision does not clarify the focus's religious or social dynamics.
Its surah proximity does not create a substantive link to the focus's leaders or idols.
Human desire to continue in wrongdoing is only a broad parallel to the alleged intention in the focus.
Patience for the Lord directly contrasts patience commanded for the gods.
Naming the Lord of Moses and Aaron completes the one-Lord confession that opposes plural worship.
Patient, God-conscious endurance resists hostile plotting, providing an opposed model of steadfastness.
Replacement of a people does not clarify the focus's collective command or alleged plan.
Forgiveness and return in a later Davud passage are unrelated to the focus's dispute.
Patient reliance on God contrasts with the focus's instruction to endure for their gods.
The shared movement verb and attributed intention occur in an unrelated journey narrative.
The approaching event has no material connection to the focus's themes.
Desire for displayed worldly advantage is only a broad form of socially shared motivation.
Different created modes of walking do not illuminate the leaders' command to proceed.
The highest assembly shares the elite term but concerns a distinct heavenly dispute.
Intention directed solely to God provides a remote ethical contrast to loyalty directed to gods.
God's lack of need from creatures is not a substantive parallel to the focus's alleged purpose.
It rejects multiplying inward authority and exposes mere verbal claims, usefully contrasting plural divine allegiance.
A marriage-work agreement and its stated benevolence are unrelated to the focus.
Self-interested desire to alter God's word is a limited parallel to imputing a calculated purpose.
Iblis declares an intent to mislead, but the setting lacks the focus's public leadership and idols.
An observer imputes a domineering intention to Moses, directly resembling the focus's suspicious passive framing.
Opponents test a messenger's ordinary life and the verse calls for patience, countering their disparagement.
All appear before the one, overpowering God, decisively contradicting the focus's plural gods.
God's command immediately realizes what He wills, strongly countering the opponents' vague claim of an intended scheme.
Divergence after clear signs is a broad parallel to communal resistance, without the focus's specific motifs.
Iblis's arrogance in a later surah scene does not clarify the focus's collective appeal.
Ineffective patience after judgment contrasts only distantly with the focus's present command to endure.
A slanderer who moves among people offers a faint parallel to leaders spreading a hostile message.
Pharaoh's self-deification is an acute expression of the false divine authority opposed by the focus's monotheism.
Seeking worldly reward is a broad instance of desire, not the focus's contested collective purpose.
Patience after condemnation is powerless, only distantly contrasting the strategic patience urged in the focus.
Davud's command to judge justly and avoid desire is unrelated to the focus's scene.
A personal promise of patience is too general to clarify its collective idolatrous deployment.
Moderation in walking has only a lexical connection to the command to walk on.
A concealed repayment designed to prompt return is unrelated to the focus's religious conflict.
Wanting God and the hereafter offers a remote contrast to desiring preservation of established gods.
It states that associating partners with God nullifies deeds, directly rejecting the focus's allegiance.
The surah's final judgment of Satan and his followers gives a consequential counterpoint to collective following.
The son's willing obedience and promised patience model steadfastness submitted to divine command.
Remembering God after a satanic prompting does not clarify the focus's leaders or their message.
Patience before hostile speech gives a direct but differently situated countermodel to the focus's endurance command.
A judgment-day rebuke for denial has no specific link to the focus's conflict.
It scales patience into mutual steadfastness and guarding together, sharply paralleling the focus's collective mobilization.
The division between believers and disbelievers does not clarify the focus's rhetoric or action.
Beautiful patience in response to a false account contrasts with persistence around a false religious order.
Distance from punishment for those promised goodness does not illuminate the focus.
The surah later commands patience in response to what opponents say, directly answering the hostile speech of this passage.
The statement that the messenger is on a straight path is too general for this workflow link.
Patience grounded in God's true promise counters being unsettled by doubters, relevant to the focus's resistance.
Pharaoh's elite urge him to leave Moses and his people to abandon Pharaoh and his gods, directly joining elite counsel and defense of gods.
Noah describes a people following leaders whose wealth and children increase their loss, supplying the leadership context for the later command not to leave gods.
Their leaders devise a great plot immediately before the collective instruction to retain the gods.
A town's elites invoke inherited custom to reject a messenger, closely paralleling the focus's leadership preserving the established religious order.
The messenger challenges whether inherited guidance remains binding even when a more guiding message arrives, directly answering elite traditionalism.
The people reject worship of God alone and defend named worship that they and their fathers instituted.
Abraham asks why his people remain devoted to the statues they continually attend.
Abraham declares an intended action against their idols after they turn away, reversing the focus's protective commitment.
He exposes the idols' inability to benefit or harm, directly undermining perseverance for their sake.
The rebuke of worshipping what neither benefits nor harms directly contests loyalty to gods.
Abraham asks his people what they worship, opening the sustained examination of inherited idol devotion.
They answer that they worship idols and remain continually devoted to them, directly paralleling steadfast attachment.
Abraham tests whether the idols can benefit or harm, challenging the value of their collective loyalty.
They take gods besides God hoping for help, directly explaining the protective allegiance urged in the focus.
The question about false gods besides God directly opposes the focus's plural divine commitment.
Abraham challenges worship of what they themselves carve, directly discrediting such gods.
The rebuke of calling on Baal while abandoning the best Creator directly counters endurance for a god.
Those taking protectors besides God justify them as means of nearness, a central rationale for rival worship.
It challenges whether the invoked beings besides God can remove harm or withhold mercy.
The challenge asks what alleged partners created and what share they possess, directly testing rival gods' authority.
The named goddesses introduce a direct catalogue of the plural deities defended by the focus's rhetoric.
It calls such gods merely names invented by people and their fathers, directly exposing inherited divine claims.
People worship what neither harms nor benefits and claim intercession, directly challenging attachment to other gods.
Associators invoke divine will to excuse their worship, a related rhetorical attribution of purpose and necessity.
They take gods besides God seeking honor, directly revealing a social motive for preserving rival worship.
It declares that the only god is God, whose knowledge encompasses all things, directly overturning plural worship.
It rejects gods besides God that create nothing and cannot control harm, benefit, death, life, or resurrection.
It identifies idol worship and fabrication of lies, linking false claims to devotion to objects besides God.
It depicts idols as a bond of worldly affection among the people, directly illuminating the focus's social cohesion around gods.
The alleged partners besides God possess no weight in heaven or earth and no share in either.
Abraham confronts his father over taking idols as gods, directly questioning plural worship.
The alleged gods besides God cannot remove or redirect harm, directly undermining reliance on them.
